newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian bonds whipped around on wages outcome.
newsitem.headline: Australian bonds whipped around on wages outcome.

text.p: *Australian bonds whipped around after the final first quarter wages data left the market still debating the chances of an easing, although the outcome lent towards unchanged policy.
*Treasury Sec Evans to deliver speech 12.30 p.m. (0230 GMT).

Australian bonds were whipped around after the final first quarter wages data left the market still debating the chances of an easing, although analysts said on balance the outcome leaned towards an unchanged policy.

All eyes were on the private sector wages outcome, which came in at a much stronger that expected at 1.3 percent, and on its own would have completely wiped the slate of thoughts of an easing in current 6.0 percent official interest rates.
But overall final average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) were revised down to 1.0 percent from a preliminary 1.3 percent, taking the annual rate to 4.3 percent.
The revision takes the annual growth rate back below the Reserve Bank's so-called "line in the sand" at 4.5 percent.

Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane has repeatedly expressed his concerns over wages growth, and while he may be slightly more comfortable with 4.3 percent, he may still be fretting over the jump in private sector growth, analysts said.

"The data still makes the market quite messy. The leads from the U.S. aren't overly helpful and we now have a whole swag of very important data running into mid June," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia.

This data includes first quarter GDP and is components, April retail trade and the May labour force report. "Running into that there has has to be very little chance of the Reserve Bank getting up in early June and cutting rates," Roberts added.
The June 10-year bond futures contract sank to 92.250 on the wages data, but subsequently bounced, while June bill futures fell to 94.01 before rebounding to 94.06.
Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Ted Evans was due to deliver a post-budget speech to Australian business economists in Sydney during the market's lunchtime recess.

Spreads to the U.S. narrowed after starting the day little changed, while they turned mixed against Canada after underperforming initially. Canadian debt continued to benefit from the Fed's stable policy and pushed the 30-year yield spread to the U.S. to a new low of three basis points on Wednesday.
